Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (AE), Diego Alvarez (SE), Priya Nair (SE), Jordan Lee (Product), SE Cohort (12)

Summary (auto): Quick refresher, then two demo rehearsals, then Q&A and action items.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, uh, we're going to run through messaging then do two demo runs, one focused on a latency-sensitive web app and another on a batch embedding pipeline, cool?
00:12 Diego: (laughs) Diego here, can everyone mute if not speaking, please?
00:18 Priya: yep, muted.
00:22 Maya: quick housekeeping -- slide deck is in the chat, link: /deck/se-messaging-v3, also recorded.
00:28 Jordan: i just want to flag, product updated the kv cache perf numbers yesterday so use the new numbers in demos, Diego i'll send that spreadsheet.
00:36 Diego: great thanks.
00:40 Maya: ok first, two minute quick pitch refresh, who wants to take a stab? Priya?
00:45 Priya: Sure. Redwood is a developer-first inference platform that makes serving LLMs predictable and economical. We help teams get consistent latency and cost across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, so you don't have to build your own infra or manage multiple runtimes.
01:05 Maya: nice, call out SLOs in the second sentence, like, low-latency for interactive, predictable throughput for batch, secure private deployments for regulated customers.
01:12 Priya: yep.
01:15 Jordan: also emphasize autoscaling and fallback policies, customers care about graceful degradation when a region spikes.
01:22 Diego: and the cost controls — batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization recommendations — those are huge for finance teams. Make it concrete with an example: "we reduced per-token cost by 30% on a support use case via caching and batching".
01:40 Maya: good. Now competitive bits — what do we say when folks ask why not OpenAI or Anthropic?
01:46 Diego: typical: OpenAI is great for quick start but customers hit limits on custom routing, private deployment, and predictable latencies. Redwood wins when you need production-grade SLA, private VPC, or dedicated capacity. Anthropic is often called out for safety but they don't offer the same deployment flexibility.
02:02 Priya: also call out model catalog and compiled runtime — we pick kernels per-hardware to squeeze latency out, that's a clear technical differentiator in deep dives.
02:12 Maya: ok let's practice an objection: "we're worried about cost vs lat—" Priya you play the customer.
02:18 Priya (as customer): "we're worried about cost, if you do caching and batching aren't we just delaying responses?"
02:22 Diego: answer: "good question. caching reduces repeated context cost and batching improves throughput without impacting tail latency for single-user interactive flows because we route latency-sensitive requests to low-latency pools and batch background jobs separately."
02:38 Priya: okay that was good, but watch the jargon, say "interactive user flows" not "single-user interactive".
02:44 Maya: nice. Alright, demo run 1: latency-sensitive web app. Diego you're on. We'll use the checkout flow example from the deck.
02:52 Diego: start demo, share screen, opening the app, hitting the product search, streaming response enabled. Quick note: the runtime demo will show model fallback to a smaller quantized variant if the primary pool is saturated — that's in the demo script.
03:06 (23s) Speaker 4: small audio glitch, can still see screen.
03:10 Diego: okay running a search, see streaming tokens come back, 180ms p50 on this local demo, and p95 around 420ms in this environment, those numbers are using our kernel-optimized path on A100 equivalent hardware per the spreadsheet.
03:25 Priya: record that as talking point: "p50 180ms, p95 < 500ms for short sequences on dedicated pools".
03:30 Maya: customer question: what if peak traffic doubles?
03:33 Diego: we have autoscaling policies and burst pools; plus smart routing to lower-cost pools for async work. In practice you can set a hard SLO and an overflow policy to route to a compatible model variant. // slight stutter: "compat-variant" mis-said as "com-pat"
03:52 Maya: good. Move to demo 2: batch embedding pipeline. Priya take this one.
03:57 Priya: sharing screen -- this is a batch job that runs nightly with 500k rows, we demonstrate dedup + prefix caching plus batching that reduces tokens processed; show cost delta vs naive run. Running job... it's completing, total runtime 22m on dedicated pool; with our batching and quantization suggestions cost dropped by ~40%.
04:22 Jordan: shoutout add a slide showing cost per embedding and absolute runtime numbers for buyers to understand economics.
04:30 Diego: note for SEs: if they ask about security, mention SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS for customer-managed keys, and audit logs — we have enterprise packages for Private.
04:42 Maya: ok let's do lightning Q&A from cohort.
04:45 SE1: question: do you show customers the actual fallback model or just logs?
04:49 Diego: we show the routing policy and can surface which variant served a request in logs and tracing; for privacy reasons we don't route PII to public hosted without consent — but in Dedicated/Private the customer owns the keys.
04:59 SE2: question: how to frame model updates/rollouts?
05:03 Priya: say: we support version pinning and can do canary rollouts with gradual traffic shifts plus automatic rollback on quality regressions, and hook to evals.
05:12 Maya: wrap up with recap.
05:15 Maya: Recap: 1) Use SLOB hooks in opening pitch (Scalability, Latency, Observability, Billing). 2) Demo scripts: have p50/p95 numbers, show autoscale and fallback. 3) Competitive: emphasize deployment flexibility and predictable economics. 4) Action items: Maya will update slides, Diego will create demo scenarios for practice, Priya will draft objection playbook.
05:36 Diego: cool. any final thoughts?
05:38 Jordan: remember to use the updated kv numbers in the sheet.
05:41 Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites for 1:1 practice slots.
05:45 (end)
